title: Deploy watchman as managed, monitorable user service; add root-guard so it never crawls ~/src wholesale
description:
`watchman.srv.pb` and `watchman.src.pb` already exist, but the **running** watchman is the ad-hoc auto-started daemon from `/usr/local/src/watchman-git` (socket at `.../var/run/watchman/rektide-state/sock`), NOT the `SYSTEMD_SERVICES` unit `watchman.srv.pb` defines. On 2026-07-24 that ad-hoc daemon got **poisoned** (watchman's term) and froze every `jj status` / `jj commit` across every `~/src` project.

## Incident (root cause)

`jj` uses watchman as its fsmonitor backend (`fsmonitor.backend = "watchman"`). Watchman resolves `watch-project ~/src/<repo>` **UP to `/home/rektide/src`** because `~/src` is itself a `.git` + `.jj` repo (history: `init`, `bd init: initialize beads issue tracking` — abandoned, no `.beads/`). It then crawls the entire src tree as one root (341k+ files under `opencode-provider-metrics` alone, ~135 watched roots), exhausts `fs.inotify.max_user_watches` (1M), and enters poison state where every request errors / hangs. jj connects, sends `watch-project`, and blocks forever on the socket read.

The `~/src` parent repo is a footgun for any VCS-aware tool, not just watchman.

## Scope

1. **Deploy the service.** Make `watchman.srv.pb` the actually-running, `systemctl --user`-managed watchman (known state/log/pid/socket layout, restartable, journalable) instead of the ad-hoc auto-started daemon.
2. **Root-guard.** Configure watchman so `watch-project ~/src/<repo>` resolves to that repo (or its real VCS root), **never** to `/home/rektide/src`. Confirm whether this build (HEAD `54602bc`, ver `20260708`) climbs to `.git`/`.jj` by default and whether `.watchmanconfig` / global `root_files` / `enforce_root_files` overrides it. Add `ignore_dirs` for build trees (`node_modules`, `target`, `.build`, `build`, `dist`, `.next`, `.cache`, `.turbo`).
3. **Monitoring.** Surface watchman health (poison state, root count, per-root watch count) alongside the existing sysctl/inotify monitoring (`status-sysctl.ts`, `files/fs-inotify/usage.sh`).
4. **Docs.** Note the `~/src` parent-repo footgun in the playbook header.

## Acceptance

- `systemctl --user status watchman` shows the active managed service from `watchman.srv.pb`.
- `watchman watch-project ~/src/<repo>` resolves to that repo, never `/home/rektide/src`.
- A poison/pressure signal is visible in the monitoring surface.
- `jj status` is fast and never hangs after a clean watchman (re)start.

title: tmux session persistence (resurrect + continuum)
description:
Add tmux-resurrect (save/restore engine) and tmux-continuum (auto-save scheduler) to the tpm-ahiru playbook so tmux sessions survive restarts.

Behavior: continuum auto-saves every 15 min but does NOT auto-restore on server start (sessions are not auto-loaded); restore is manual via a restore-session.sh bin or the resurrect keybinding. Snapshots land at the XDG data-home canonical path ~/.local/share/tmux/resurrect.
notes:
## What was done

Added to `tpm-ahiru.src.pb`:

- **Plugins** (`ahiru-plugins.conf`): `tmux-plugins/tmux-resurrect` (the save/restore engine) + `tmux-plugins/tmux-continuum` (auto-save scheduler built on resurrect).
- **New config file** `ahiru-resurrect.conf`: `@continuum-restore 'off'` (no auto-load on server start), `@continuum-save-interval '15'` (keeps saving), `@resurrect-capture-pane-contents 'on'`. Wired into `install-user.sh` as a third `block-in-file` block between plugins and the init line.
- **New bin** `restore-session.sh`: manually loads the last resurrect snapshot. Guards for an active tmux session, locates the restore script via `TMUX_PLUGIN_MANAGER_PATH` (fallback `~/.tmux/plugins`), invokes via `tmux run-shell`.
- **Snapshot path** set to the XDG data-home canonical `~/.local/share/tmux/resurrect`. Confirmed via upstream `docs/save_dir.md` that resurrect only supports `$HOME`, `$HOSTNAME` and `~` (no shell/env interpolation), so `$XDG_DATA_HOME` had to be written out by its default.

Committed as kypkzqyn.

## How it takes effect

Nothing is live until the playbook runs. Flow:

1. `ansible-playbook -i 'localhost,' -c local tpm-ahiru.src.pb -e USERMODE=True` — generates etc/ + bin/
2. `install-user.sh` — splices plugins/resurrect/run blocks into `~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf` (or `~/.tmux.conf`)
3. `ahiru-tpm install` — clones the plugins
4. tmux server start reads the conf -> continuum auto-saves every 15 min. Auto-restore is OFF by design, so starting tmux does not load a session.

For a current session: after 1-3, `tmux source-file ~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf` to load plugin settings into the live server, then `restore-session.sh` (or `prefix Ctrl-r`) to load the last snapshot.

## Caveat to verify live

ahiru-tpm's plugin install path was assumed to be the TPM-standard `~/.tmux/plugins` (overridable via `TMUX_PLUGIN_MANAGER_PATH`). If ahiru uses a different default, adjust the fallback in `restore-session.sh`.

## Evaluation / follow-up

- **Named snapshots**: resurrect keeps only `last` + `prev`. Multiple named/rotating snapshots would need a wrapper bin that copies files out of `@resurrect-dir`. Easy to layer on top of restore-session.sh.
- **Shared snapshot path**: `@resurrect-dir` could point at a synced/host-shared location to carry sessions across machines.

title: zim: env module — declarative env-var zimfw module
description:
Add a new zim module kind `env` that generates a zimfw-loadable env-setting script from a mapping, replacing bespoke per-playbook .zsh scripts.

## Why
The local-file module kind (`source: foo.zsh`) requires authoring a repo script for the common case of "export a few env vars at shell startup". watchman currently ships files/watchman/watchman-env.zsh purely to export WATCHMAN_SOCK with the don't-stomp + COMPFUZOR_ENV_OVERWRITE convention. That convention should be standardized and auto-generated, not hand-copied per service.

## Design
A ZIM_MODULE entry may declare `env` (a mapping of VAR -> value) instead of `source`:

  ZIM_MODULES:
    - name: watchman-env
      phase: tools
      env:
        WATCHMAN_SOCK: "{{VAR}}/sock"

zim_fragment treats an `env` entry as a local zimfw module (like the .zsh file kind): it renders an init.zsh under {{ETC}}/zim-modules/<name>/ whose content is GENERATED from the mapping (one don't-stomp guard per var), and emits a `zmodule <etc>/zim-modules/<name>` declaration. The init.zsh content follows the gen_bins COMPFUZOR_ENV_OVERWRITE convention (already documented in gen_bins.tasks):

  if [ -z "${WATCHMAN_SOCK:-}" ] || [ -n "${COMPFUZOR_ENV_OVERWRITE:-}" ]; then
    export WATCHMAN_SOCK="<value>"
  fi

So `env` produces an init.zsh with generated `content`, whereas the file kind produces one with `src` — env replaces the bespoke src script for the env-setting case.

## Scope
1. zim_fragment: add `env` kind (mapping) alongside `file` (.zsh/file:true) and `git` (url) kinds. Require `name` for env modules (no source to slug from). Render per-var don't-stomp guards with COMPFUZOR_ENV_OVERWRITE.
2. Tests: cover env-kind declaration filename, generated init.zsh content, multi-var, disabled, missing-name rejection.
3. watchman: drop files/watchman/watchman-env.zsh; switch its ZIM_MODULE from `source: watchman-env.zsh` to `env: {WATCHMAN_SOCK: "{{VAR}}/sock"}`.

## Acceptance
- An `env:` ZIM_MODULE renders a local zimfw module whose init.zsh exports the vars without stomping (forced by COMPFUZOR_ENV_OVERWRITE).- watchman.srv.pb has no bespoke .zsh script and no block-in-file; its shell integration is fully declared via `env`.
- zim_fragment tests pass; watchman renders + install-user-zimfw.sh still composed.
notes:
Implemented:
- qkppssru bins: resolve `../` bin src without files/<TYPE>/ (enabler -- watchman ships no files/watchman/ now)
- msnptkpl zim: env module kind (zim_fragment env|file|git + tests; gen_zim module-dir derivation by name)
- usmwzxtv watchman: switch shell integration to the env zim module (drops files/watchman/watchman-env.zsh)

Verified: 46 zim_fragment tests pass; full filter/lookup suite green; watchman renders the generated env init.zsh ({{VAR}} resolved, don't-stomp + COMPFUZOR_ENV_OVERWRITE), the zmodule abspath declaration, and auto install-user-zimfw.sh.

title: First-class modprobe non-options directives (blacklist/softdep/install/remove/alias)
description:
## Problem

The kernel_modprobe subsystem (`files/kernel/build-kernel.sh`, `install-kernel.sh`)
only emits `options <mod> k=v ...` lines, derived from `KERNEL_MODULES.<mod>.params`.
Every other modprobe.d directive has no first-class primitive, so playbooks hand-roll
a raw fragment via `ETC_FILES` + `LINKS` into `/etc/modprobe.d/` (pstore.etc.pb itself
documents this gap at pstore.etc.pb:152-154: "compfuzor has no first-class blacklist
primitive"). That bypasses the kernel subsys entirely: no build/install script, no
status reporting, no idempotent managed link.

## Proposal

A first-class modprobe primitive for non-`options` directives. Suggested shape (open
to design): a `KERNEL_MODPROBE` (or `MODPROBE_LINES`) mapping that takes directive
types and materializes `/etc/modprobe.d/<NAME>.conf` via the existing kernel subsys
install path (managed symlink, status surfaced), e.g.

    KERNEL_MODPROBE:
      blacklist:
        - efi_pstore
      softdep:
        - module: mymod
          pre: "drm"

Directive types to support: `blacklist`, `softdep`, `install`, `remove`, `alias`
(`options` stays owned by `KERNEL_MODULES`).

## Playbooks this fixes

- **pstore.etc.pb** (blacklist `efi_pstore`) -- the motivating case; currently
  hand-linked via `ETC_FILES` + `LINKS` at pstore.etc.pb:155-165. Once landed, drop
  the manual `ETC_FILES`/`LINKS` and declare it through the primitive.
- **udlfb** (`files/udlfb.plugable/fbconf.conf` blacklists `font`/`tileblit`/
  `bitblit`/`fbcon`) -- fragment exists but `udlfb.pb` is currently an empty stub
  (0 lines), so this also needs the playbook itself to be written.

## Acceptance

- A playbook can declare `blacklist`/`softdep`/`install`/`remove`/`alias` directives.
- `install-kernel.sh` (module mode) materializes them into `/etc/modprobe.d/<NAME>.conf`
  as a managed symlink, alongside any `options` from `KERNEL_MODULES`.
- A status reporter reflects them so `status.sh` can show drift.
- pstore.etc.pb migrated off its hand-rolled `LINKS`.

title: python via mise python + uv
description:
Run the project's Python via mise-managed python + uv, building on the
`mise.toml` tool/version support (`compfuzor-mise-toml`).

## Scope
- Declare `python` (+ `uv`) as mise-managed tools in the generated `mise.toml`
  so the project's Python is provisioned by `mise install` rather than relying
  on a system python or a hand-rolled venv/pyenv.
- Wire the python subsystem's build/install to run under that mise python with
  uv (`uv sync` / `uv pip` style), so both the toolchain and the runtime come
  from mise.
- Result: a self-contained, reproducible Python toolchain per project -- no
  system-python or pyenv dependency, versions pinned in `mise.toml`.

Depends on `compfuzor-mise-toml` (the `mise.toml` + `mise install` foundation).

title: gen_link subsystem: reify link specs into generated build-*/install-* scripts
description:
## Problem

Compfuzor has two ways to put a generated file into a system location, and
neither is generative:

1. **`LINKS`** (the ansible variable) — creates symlinks **inline during the
   ansible run** (`tasks/compfuzor/links.tasks`). This is explicitly deprecated
   (`links.tasks:2-8`): it drags system-mutating work into ansible's compile
   phase, needs `become`, and can't be re-run as a standalone tool.

2. **Hand-written `install-*.sh` BINS** — the idiomatic modern pattern
   (bluetooth.etc.pb, git.etc.pb, kernel `install-sysctl.sh`). Each playbook
   hand-writes the `ln -sfv`/`mkdir`/`dconf update` logic itself. There is no
   declarative input that *generates* the linking script — the author rewrites
   the same `sudo ln -sfv "$DIR/etc/x" "/etc/..."` boilerplate every time.

What's missing is a **generative link layer**: a declaration that says "this
ETC_FILE should appear at `/etc/dconf/db/gdm.d/00-no-suspend`" and have the
framework *reify* that into the right script, in the right phase, with the
right transport.

## Vision: `gen_link`

A subsystem/filter (mirroring `gen_bins` / `bin_composers`) that takes
declarative link specs and emits them into generated `build-*.sh` or
`install-*.sh` scripts. gen_bins already composes those action scripts into
`build.sh` / `install.sh` umbrellas — gen_link *feeds* them instead of each
playbook hand-writing the symlink body.

Two independent, switchable axes:

### Axis 1 — transport (runtime): link vs copy

- **link** (default): `ln -sfv "$DIR/etc/<file>" "<dest>"` — the live file
  tracks the compfuzor-managed source. This is the current idiom.
- **copy** (opt-in, NOT run by default): `cp -v "$DIR/etc/<file>" "<dest>"` —
  the deployed file is a snapshot. Useful when the target must not be a symlink
  (e.g. daemons that refuse to follow symlinks, or read-only mounts that can't
  reach back into `/etc/opt`).

This is a **runtime** switch: the generated install script branches on an env
var, so the same generated artifact can deploy either way without regenerating.

### Axis 2 — phase (compile-time): build-* vs install-*

A link spec can be routed into either action family:

- **install-\<name\>.sh** (default): deploy to the system (symlink/copy into
  `/etc/...`, reload). The current model.
- **build-\<name\>.sh**: prepare/assemble at build time (e.g. stage a file into
  a layer that a separate installer consumes). Rare, but some subsystems want
  linking to happen pre-deploy.

This is a **compile-time** switch: it decides *which script filename* gen_link
emits into, so gen_bins' compositor picks it up under the right umbrella. It is
not something the runtime script can branch on.

## Naming

Per the prototype work in `gdm-no-suspend.etc.pb`, two options for the suffix:

- **`-<name>`** (preferred if we can swing it): `build-dconf.sh` /
  `install-dconf.sh`, where `<name>` is the link-group (the dconf target here).
  Matches the existing `build-sysctl.sh` / `install-sysctl.sh` kernel
  convention. gen_bins' `_ACTION_PATTERN` already matches
  `install-<name>[.user].sh`.
- **explicitly named**: each spec declares its target script name explicitly.
  More verbose, but unambiguous when one script aggregates several unrelated
  links.

## Inputs (sketch)

```yaml
LINK_SPECS:                # or fold into LINKS with generative shape
  - src: 00-no-suspend      # ETC_FILES name under $DIR/etc
    dest: /etc/dconf/db/gdm.d/00-no-suspend
    transport: link         # link (default) | copy
    phase: install          # install (default) | build
    name: dconf             # -> install-dconf.sh / build-dconf.sh
    after:                  # post-link commands (reload, etc)
      - dconf update
```

gen_link would co-author these into `install-<name>.sh` / `build-<name>.sh`
BINS, which gen_bins then composes into the umbrella `install.sh` / `build.sh`.

## Relationship to existing work

- **Extends / supersedes `compfuzor-links-install-sh`** — that ticket proposed
  "LINKS should co-author install.sh". gen_link generalizes it: any link spec
  feeds a generated action script (not just the umbrella install.sh), across
  both build/install phases, with a link/copy transport switch.
- **Parallel to `gen_bins`** (`compfuzor-gen-bins`) — gen_bins composes
  *existing* action scripts; gen_link *authors* link-deployment action scripts
  for gen_bins to compose. They are complementary halves.
- **Mirror of the `config` drift subsystem** (`compfuzor-config-drift`) — that
  subsystem moved hand-written config-assembly into a generative layer with
  desired-vs-deployed drift. gen_link does the same for the deploy/transport
  step.

## Prototype

`gdm-no-suspend.etc.pb` is a worked prototype: it hand-writes the
`install-dconf.sh` body that gen_link would generate, layers on a runtime
copy/link branch (env-gated), and carries commented-out ENVs sketching the
phase (build/install) and transport (link/copy) switches that the subsystem
would consume. See that playbook for the concrete shape this ticket proposes.
notes: Prototype evolved: the gdm-no-suspend target is Debian's greeter.dconf-defaults conffile (a shared dpkg-managed file, not a .d slot), so neither 'link' nor 'copy' transport fits — the deploy is a 'merge' (crudini --merge of a generated keyfile into the conffile). gen_link should support a third transport: merge (key-level overlay into an existing file), alongside link (symlink) and copy (clobber). This is the conffile case; link/copy remain right for .d-directory and standalone-file targets.

title: per-language COMMENT vars across gen build subsystems
description:
Per-language `COMMENT` vars let each build subsystem (rust, make, python, ...)
annotate the action scripts gen_bins composes from it, so a generated
`build.sh` / `install.sh` carries a comment header explaining what it runs
(e.g. `cargo build`, `make install`) instead of being opaque.

## Capability
- `<LANG>_COMMENT` / `<LANG>_COMMENT_INSTALL` vars (e.g. `RUST_COMMENT`,
  `RUST_COMMENT_INSTALL`, `MAKE_COMMENT_INSTALL`) consumed by the build
  subsystems and rendered into the generated bin bodies.
- Generalized in "build subsystems: suffixed bin names + per-language COMMENT
  vars" so each language subsystem contributes its own comment lines uniformly.
- Pairs with suffixed bin names (`build-<lang>.sh`) so each language's build
  step is a distinct, self-describing compositor member.

## Why it matters
Generated action scripts are read by humans (debugging, auditing). Per-language
comment vars make them legible at a glance -- you see what runs and why, per
subsystem, without reading the bin body.

## Followups
- Roll out COMMENT vars to the remaining build subsystems that lack them
  (go, bazel, nodejs, bun, ...).
- Maybe a shared helper so each subsystem doesn't re-implement the
  comment-rendering snippet.

title: [epic] config subsystem drift detection
description:
compfuzor's `config` subsystem assembles a config file from fragments (the
`config-<merge>.sh` mergers driven by `CONFIG_KEY`) and installs it -- and now
it also knows when the deployed file has drifted from the desired assembly, not
just how to write it.

## Capability
- `--check` drift mode: report desired-vs-deployed without installing; normalized
  `CONFIG_OUTPUT` path handling.
- `status-config.sh` reporter registered through `gen_status`, so `status.sh`
  surfaces config drift alongside the kernel/sysctl reporters.
- Quiet by default: silent on no-change, shows a diff when the assembly actually
  changes on install; `block-in-file` chatter silenced in `--check`.

## Why it matters
This is the same desired-vs-deployed drift pattern as the kernel status
reporters (`status-modules`, `status-cmdline`), applied to assembled config
files. A config managed by compfuzor becomes self-describing: `status.sh` tells
you whether the live file matches what the playbook declares, and `--check`
does it as a one-shot. Closes the loop from "generate + install" to
"generate + install + verify".

## Pieces
- `config.sh` / `config-yaml-list.sh` (and other mergers) -- assemble the file.
- `--check` mode + `CONFIG_OUTPUT` normalization.
- `status-config.sh` reporter (via `gen_status` -> `STATUSES`).
- install-time diff/silence behavior.

## Possible followups
- Generalize the drift-reporter shape so other assembled-file subsystems reuse it.
- Unify with the `status-*.ts` three-way (desired/deployed/live) vocabulary where it fits.

title: [epic] gen_bins action-combiner subsystem
description:
gen_bins is compfuzor's action-composition layer: it turns a pile of
individually-authored `build-*.sh` / `install-*.sh` scripts into one compositor
entry point per (action, scope) -- `build.sh`, `install.sh`, `install-user.sh`,
... -- each carrying a `run_all` of its members. The combiner at its heart is
quietly one of the nicest pieces in the framework.

## How it fits together
- `bin_composers.py` (the filter) scans `BINS` for action scripts matching
  `build|install[-scope][.user].sh`, groups them by (action, scope), and emits
  one compositor per group whose `run_all` is the ordered member list. Library
  scripts opt out with `compose: false`; subsystem-generated compositors are
  excluded from re-composition via `generated_by: gen_bins`.
- `gen_kernel`/other gens contribute action members; `gen_bins.tasks` runs the
  filter and merges the synthesized compositors back into `BINS`.
- `files/_bin` renders each compositor's body: header (env sourcing, setopt
  stack) -> the `run_all` loop (`"$DIR/bin/<member>" "$@"`) -> footer (option
  restore). The same template renders every generated bin.
- `bins.tasks` deploys them; `bins_run.tasks` runs any with `args`/`run`/`become`
  at apply time.

## Why it's valuable
Adding `install-foo.sh` to a config automatically extends `install.sh` for the
right scope, in the right place, with announce/ordering handled for free. Action
scripts stay single-purpose and individually testable; the compositor is
generated, never hand-maintained. Subsystems (kernel_modprobe, kernel_params,
kernel_bls, ...) just contribute their own `install-*.sh` members and the
combiner does the rest -- including scoping (`install-user.sh` /
`install-*.user.sh` infer the `user` scope) and dedup against gen_bins output.

## Recent extensions (this work)
- `run_all` announce: each member prints `+ <name>` before running and
  `complete` after; suppressible via `COMPFUZOR_QUIET` or `V=0` (unset/empty
  stays loud).
- `kernel_bls` subsys contributes `install-kernel-bls.sh` as a composed member
  ordered last (BLS regen after the cmdline writers), replacing a special-cased
  template fragment / `bin_composers` domain flag -- the combiner absorbed it
  cleanly with no composer change.
- Status reporters (`status-cmdline.ts`, `status-ramoops.sh`, ...) ride the same
  BINS mechanism into `bin/` and `status.sh`'s `REPORTERS`.

## Possible followups
- Finer-grained `_bin` insertion points (`pre_run` / `final`) for explicit
  run_all-relative placement, so framework-injected tail steps and playbook
  custom steps get named slots instead of relying on BINS-list order.
- `.ts` reporters announce fine but crash under `sudo`'s `secure_path` node (no
  type-stripping); a `COMPFUZOR_NODE` or `--experimental-strip-types` invocation
  in `status.sh` would make them sudo-safe.

title: Route subsystem TOOL_VERSIONS into mise.toml when MISE_VERSIONS is set
description: MISE_VERSIONS doubles as the mise-mode signal. When set, the union of TOOL_VERSIONS and MISE_VERSIONS renders to mise.toml only and no .tool-versions is emitted, so subsystem tool requirements (e.g. python: true) follow the playbook into mise. MISE_VERSIONS wins on conflicts; unresolved true resolves to latest in the mise renderer. Legacy .tool-versions is unchanged when MISE_VERSIONS is absent.
acceptance_criteria: A playbook with MISE_VERSIONS set emits only mise.toml (union of TOOL_VERSIONS + MISE_VERSIONS); no .tool-versions link. A playbook without MISE_VERSIONS emits .tool-versions as before. solstone.src.pb produces mise.toml with python and uv, no .tool-versions.
notes: Verified: ran tests/filter_plugins/merge.test.py (27 passed, added test_merge_dict_tool_versions_mise_union) and isolated ansible-playbook runs of gen_tool_versions.tasks. MISE mode (TOOL_VERSIONS python:true + MISE_VERSIONS uv:latest) -> only mise.toml with python="latest" and uv="latest". Legacy mode (no MISE_VERSIONS) -> only .tool-versions. solstone.src.pb --syntax-check clean. Docs updated in doc/subsys.md; README test count bumped.
close_reason: Shipped in jj commit 0c05610b. gen_tool_versions.tasks: MISE_VERSIONS gates mise-mode; union of TOOL_VERSIONS+MISE_VERSIONS renders to mise.toml only; true->latest in mise renderer; legacy .tool-versions unchanged when MISE_VERSIONS absent.

title: mise.toml tool/version support
description:
One feature: compfuzor's version-manager emits `mise.toml` (not
`.tool-versions`) to declare project tool versions, and provisions those tools
via `mise install` at install time. Subsystems contribute their tool
requirements into a single merged `[tools]` table.

## Architecture (present resultant state)
- **Data shape:** `TOOL_VERSIONS` and `MISE_VERSIONS` are both `{tool:
  version}` mappings, merged with the `tool_versions_overlay` strategy
  (`single=true`). A version of `true` resolves to the `<TOOL>_VERSION` var
  (or `"latest"` under mise).
- **Output selection** (`gen_tool_versions.tasks`):
  - `MISE_VERSIONS` declared (deflengthy) -> emit `etc/mise.toml` with a
    `[tools]` table built from the MERGE of `TOOL_VERSIONS` + `MISE_VERSIONS`,
    link it into place, and add an `early: mise install` step to the generated
    `install.sh` so the tools are provisioned during install.
  - Only `TOOL_VERSIONS` -> emit the legacy `.tool-versions` instead.
  So setting `MISE_VERSIONS` is what flips the whole config from
  `.tool-versions` to `mise.toml` AND wires install-time provisioning.
- **Subsystem contributions:** each build subsystem (rust, python, go, ...)
  feeds its tool/version needs into the merged set, so `mise.toml` reflects
  every language the project actually uses.
- **Runtime integration:** mise exposes the tools' env to the session via a
  systemd user-env service (mise defines user-env through the systemd
  subsystem; env is pushed into the systemd user manager), so declared tools
  are on PATH without per-shell shimming.

## Scope
This captures the feature as it stands: `mise.toml` generation +
install-time `mise install` + the `[tools]` merge from subsystems. The earlier
`.tool-versions`-only path and the rename/bug churn are folded in / dropped;
`compfuzor-mise-version-routing` is kept as a closed record of the evolution.

title: Data-driven zim module subsystem (host/contributor fragments)
description:
Zim modules become declared data (ZIM_MODULES) rendered into phase-numbered drop-in fragments, replacing hand-maintained zmodule shell snippets. Mirrors the MCP host/contributor model: a host playbook (ZIM_HOST) owns the assembly dir + install-zim.sh bridge; any contributor declares modules that symlink into the host target.

Design:
- zim_fragment filter normalizes module entries (source/args/name/description/comment/enabled) into <num>-<name>[-<desc>].conf fragments under etc/zim/ (or etc/zim-disabled/ for enabled:false). phase is a name (core/prompt/tools/completion/late -> 20/40/55/70/85) or a number 00-99; sorted filenames give deterministic load order across independent contributors.
- gen_zim.tasks: contributor branch renders fragments + staging dirs; host branch provides install-zim.sh and exports ZIM_TARGET.
- install-zim.sh symlinks a contributor's fragments into the host's etc/zimfw/ (ZIM_TARGET sourced from env.export). Mirrors mcp-install.sh.
- zim.opt.pb rewritten as ZIM_HOST + first-contributor; the five hardcoded zimfw/*.conf become a ZIM_MODULES declaration. install-user.sh promotes via install-zim.sh before config.sh.
- Ordering is by filename, not ansible. Drift for the assembled etc/zimfw.conf is detected for free via the existing config subsystem (CONFIG_KEY: zimfw auto-registers status-config.sh, which runs config-block-in-file.sh --check to re-assemble into a temp and diff without writing).
notes:
Implemented in jj change qoqmumqq (commit 12d8c91f).

Files:
- library/filter_plugins/zim_fragment.py + tests/filter_plugins/zim_fragment.test.py (31 tests, all passing)
- tasks/compfuzor/gen_zim.tasks (contributor + host branches)
- files/install-zim.sh (symlink bridge, mirrors mcp-install.sh)
- tasks/compfuzor.includes (wired gen_zim after gen_config)
- zim.opt.pb (ZIM_HOST + ZIM_MODULES: 66 entries, 35 active / 31 disabled)

Verified:
- zim_fragment: 31/31 tests; phase name+number resolution, slug derivation (owner/repo/URL/.git), args (string+list), comment (string/multiline/list), description disambiguation, enabled->disabled dir, range/missing/bool rejection.
- Render simulation of zim.opt.pb's 66 modules: no filename collisions (zoxide variants disambiguated via description: kiesman99/vietz-dev/antoineco); sort order core(20)->prompt(40)->tools(55)->completion(70)->late(85) preserves Zim constraints (completion after --fpath contributors, syntax-highlighting last).
- install-zim.sh end-to-end: symlinks active->etc/zimfw/, disabled->etc/zimfw-disabled/, sources env.export for ZIM_TARGET.
- Full filter test suite green; YAML parses on all touched task/playbook files.

Note: README intentionally left untouched (filter is bespoke/special-purpose, not surfaced in the general filter catalog).

title: Colocate jj on all git repos after clone
description:
When compfuzor downloads a git repository (REPO, REPOS mapping, or REPOS list via tasks/compfuzor/repo_git.tasks), automatically colocate jujutsu on it (jj git init) and make an initial commit (jj commit), so every managed git clone is jj-enabled on download.

Implementation (done):
- repo_git.tasks gains a jj colocate step that runs after cloning, per repo.
- Idempotent via args.creates (skips when .jj already present).
- No-op where jj is absent (command -v jj guard), so jj-less hosts are unaffected.
- Gated by JJ_BYPASS (plus the existing GIT_BYPASS / REPO_BYPASS).
- Commit message customizable via JJ_COMMIT_MSG (default 'compfuzor: jj init').

Delivered alongside: the three git-clone paths (REPO, REPOS dict, REPOS list) were collapsed into a single normalized git_repos list driving one clone task + one jj task, so the jj step cost no extra actions.
acceptance_criteria: Every git repo fetched by repo_git.tasks has a colocated .jj and an initial jj commit after download; re-runs are no-ops; jj absent -> skipped; JJ_BYPASS opts out.
notes:
Implemented in commits on tasks/compfuzor/repo_git.tasks:
- rlxvlqvuptlr: repo_git: colocate jj and commit after git clone
- tlsrvtnqspxs: repo_git: collapse REPO/REPOS(dict)/REPOS(list) into one git_repos list
- tnulmsmovlxq: repo_git: fold REPO/REPOS normalization into a single set_fact

Captured retroactively; behavior verified via local ansible runs of all three input forms.

title: Apply _BASE pattern to all SYSTEMD_*_DEFAULT dicts
description:
## Pattern

Separate static defaults from conditional combines, as done for `SYSTEMD_SERVICES_DEFAULT_BASE` -> `SYSTEMD_SERVICES_DEFAULT` in `vars/systemd.yaml`.

## Current state

```yaml
SYSTEMD_SERVICES_DEFAULT_BASE:       # static
  Type: simple
  Restart: on-failure
  RestartSec: 5

SYSTEMD_SERVICES_DEFAULT: >-         # combines static + conditional
  {{ SYSTEMD_SERVICES_DEFAULT_BASE | combine(...) }}
```

## Candidates

- `SYSTEMD_UNITS_DEFAULT` (line 403) — has `Description: "{{ NAME }}"` which is already a Jinja expression, but could still benefit from a _BASE for static keys like `DefaultDependencies`
- `SYSTEMD_INSTALLS_DEFAULT` (line 418) — `WantedBy` is conditional on SYSTEMD_SCOPE

## Scope

This is a low-priority cleanup. Apply when touching these defaults for other reasons, or as a quick pass.

Parent: compfuzor-systemd

title: Auto-inject EnvironmentFile into generated systemd units
description:
## Problem

The systemd unit template (`files/systemd.unit`) renders section dicts but has no awareness of the generated `env.export` file. Playbooks must manually add `EnvironmentFile=` or individual `Environment=` directives.

The env file is generated from `files/_env` template and contains all playbook ENV vars (DIR, NAME, TYPE, INSTANCE, plus any custom ENV entries). It lives at `$DIR/env.export`. For systemd services that need these vars, the unit should reference it automatically.

## Current behavior

A playbook with:
```yaml
ENV:
  model: whisper-large
SYSTEMD_SERVICES:
  ExecStart: handy
```

Generates a unit with no reference to the env file. The handy service has no way to know `model=whisper-large`.

## Proposed behavior

When `SYSTEMD_SERVICE` (or any unit type) is defined and an env file is generated (`ENV` is a mapping or `ENV_LIST` is set), the unit template should automatically include:

```ini
[Service]
EnvironmentFile=-/path/to/deployment/env.export
ExecStart=handy
```

The `-` prefix (permissive) means systemd wont
notes: Implemented in vars/systemd.yaml: SYSTEMD_SERVICES_DEFAULT now conditionally includes EnvironmentFile=-<DIR>/env.export when ENV is present (mapping or boolean) or ENV_LIST is defined.

title: Add --now to install-unit.sh enable step
description:
## Problem

`files/systemd/install-unit.sh` line 20 does `$SUDO_CMD $SYSTEMCTL enable "$target"` but does not start the service. For user services especially, authors expect the service to start immediately after install.

Currently every hand-written `install-user.sh` that deals with systemd includes `systemctl --user enable --now` or a separate `systemctl --user start`. The auto-generated install scripts should match this expectation.

## Fix

In `files/systemd/install-unit.sh`, change:
```bash
$SUDO_CMD $SYSTEMCTL enable "$target"
```
to:
```bash
$SUDO_CMD $SYSTEMCTL enable --now "$target"
```

This is a one-line change in `files/systemd/install-unit.sh:20`.

## Verification

- Run a playbook that generates install-service-user.sh and confirm it starts the service
- Check that system-scope install scripts still work (sudo systemctl enable --now)

Parent: compfuzor-systemd
notes:
Updated design: --now is default. Opt-out via SYSTEMD_BYPASS_START env var. install-unit.sh checks `[ -n "$SYSTEMD_BYPASS_START" ]` and skips --now flag when set.
Also accept --bypass-start as CLI flag. install-unit.sh parses args: strip --bypass-start from $@, pass remaining args through to systemctl. Checked in order: CLI flag > SYSTEMD_BYPASS_START env var.

```bash
_bypass_start=false
_pass_through=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ "$arg" = "--bypass-start" ]; then
    _bypass_start=true
  else
    _pass_through+=("$arg")
  fi
done

if [ "$_bypass_start" = true ] || [ -n "$SYSTEMD_BYPASS_START" ]; then
  $SUDO_CMD $SYSTEMCTL enable "${_pass_through[@]}" "$target"
else
  $SUDO_CMD $SYSTEMCTL enable --now "${_pass_through[@]}" "$target"
fi
```
Implemented in files/systemd/install-unit.sh: --now is default, --bypass-start CLI flag and SYSTEMD_BYPASS_START env var for opt-out.

title: Make systemd a proper compfuzor subsystem
description:
# Systemd Subsystem Refactoring

## Current State

Systemd handling is NOT a proper subsystem in the `doc/subsys.md` sense. It has no entry in `SUBSYSTEM` in `vars/common.yaml`, no `gen_systemd.tasks`, and no `subsys` lookup integration. Instead it is a bespoke pipeline spread across 5+ files that runs unconditionally.

## Key Files

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `vars/systemd.yaml` (413 lines) | Defaults, SYSTEMD_TYPE_CONFIG (14 unit types), phrase lists, scope gates, pkg-config-derived directory paths |
| `tasks/compfuzor/vars_systemd.tasks` (33 lines) | Runs `pkg-config systemd --variable=...` for 23 paths, loads defaults |
| `tasks/compfuzor/vars_systemd_unit.tasks` (187 lines) | Monolith: type detection, ETC_FILES generation, install script generation, SYSTEMD_ROOTS multi-unit, separate system/user scope |
| `tasks/systemd.thunk.tasks` (28 lines) | Legacy enable/restart during post-run phase |
| `tasks/systemd.unit.includes` (104 lines) | Older unit generation with .d directory handling, being replaced |
| `files/systemd.unit` (22 lines) | Section-based template rendering from merged dicts |
| `files/systemd/install-unit.sh` (22 lines) | Shared install helper: symlink + daemon-reload + enable |
| `files/systemd.service` | Old phrase-based template (legacy) |
| `skill/systemd.md` (244 lines) | User-facing documentation |

## Problems

### 1. Runs unconditionally
`vars_systemd_unit.tasks` is imported at `compfuzor.includes:24` with no `when:` guard. Every playbook gets systemd processing even if it defines no units. This violates the subsystem pattern where `gen_*.tasks` should be guarded by the trigger condition.

### 2. Not a subsystem
No entry in `SUBSYSTEM` dict, no `gen_systemd.tasks`, no `subsys` lookup. The systemd "subsystem" is split between vars processing and task includes rather than following the standard pattern described in `doc/subsys.md`.

### 3. 187-line monolith in vars_systemd_unit.tasks
This single task file handles: type detection (`_systemd_has_service`, `_systemd_has_socket`, etc.), ETC_FILES generation for single units, ETC_FILES generation from SYSTEMD_ROOTS, install-unit.sh BINS injection, per-type per-scope install script generation. All of this should be decomposed.

### 4. User service install requires hand-written scripts
Of ~36 playbooks with `install-user.sh`, nearly all that deal with systemd user services hand-roll: `mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user`, symlink, daemon-reload, enable, start. The auto-generated `install-service-user.sh` exists but:
- Only enables, does not start (no `--now`)
- Is not well-known to playbook authors
- Requires understanding SYSTEMD_INSTALL=user/both/separate to trigger

### 5. install-unit.sh does not start services
The generated install scripts only `enable` units, never `enable --now` or `start`. For user services especially, authors expect the service to start immediately.

### 6. No EnvironmentFile integration
The systemd unit template (`files/systemd.unit`) renders section dicts but has no awareness of the generated `env.export` file. Playbooks must manually add `EnvironmentFile=` or `Environment=` directives. The env file (generated from `files/_env` template) contains all the playbook ENV vars and is available at `$DIR/env.export`, but the systemd unit does not reference it.

### 7. Scope confusion for non-USERMODE playbooks
Many `.src.pb` playbooks need a user systemd service but are NOT user-mode (they install binaries system-wide, need system PKGS, etc.). The current system conflates USERMODE with systemd user scope. Getting a user service in a system-mode playbook requires setting SYSTEMD_SCOPE, SYSTEMD_INSTALL, and SYSTEMD_INSTALLS.WantedBy explicitly. There is no simple "just give me a user service" affordance.

### 8. Dual codepaths
`systemd.unit.includes` (old) and `vars_systemd_unit.tasks` (new) coexist. The old path handles .d directory config overlays. The thunk.tasks still runs for enable/restart. The migration from old to new is incomplete.

## The Three-Section Dict Pattern (works well)

The current pattern of three dicts mapping to [Unit], [Service], [Install] sections is good:
- `SYSTEMD_UNITS` -> [Unit]
- `SYSTEMD_SERVICES` -> [Service] (or type-specific section)
- `SYSTEMD_INSTALLS` -> [Install]

These merge on top of defaults from `vars/systemd.yaml`. The `files/systemd.unit` template iterates section names from `SYSTEMD_TYPE_CONFIG` and renders key=value pairs. This is clean and should be preserved.

## What a Proper Subsystem Would Look Like

Following `doc/subsys.md`:

1. Add `systemd` entry to `SUBSYSTEM` in `vars/common.yaml` with:
   - `requested`: triggered by SYSTEMD_SERVICE/SOCKET/MOUNT or SYSTEMD_SERVICES/SOCKETS/MOUNTS being defined
   - `contrib`: install-unit.sh helper and generated type-specific install scripts as BINS

2. Create `gen_systemd.tasks` — merge BINS (install scripts) and ETC_FILES (unit files), guarded by `lookup(subsys, id=systemd, get=active)`

3. Guard the import in `compfuzor.includes` with `when:` matching the trigger

4. Keep `vars_systemd.tasks` (pkg-config probe) running conditionally or making paths available on-demand

5. Migrate `systemd.thunk.tasks` behavior into the generated install scripts (enable + restart)

6. Add `install-user.sh` as a generated BINS entry when user scope is active, covering the common case of: create dir, symlink unit, daemon-reload, enable --now

## Migration Path

1. Add systemd to SUBSYSTEM with requested trigger
2. Create gen_systemd.tasks with the unit generation + install script logic
3. Guard compfuzor.includes import
4. Add install-user.sh generation for user scope
5. Add EnvironmentFile= awareness to unit template
6. Retire systemd.unit.includes and systemd.thunk.tasks
7. Migrate playbooks from hand-written install-user.sh to generated one
8. Consider making install-unit.sh do enable --now by default

title: LINKS should co-author install.sh instead of requiring manual symlinks
description:
Currently LINKS creates symlinks during the filesystem phase. We want LINKS entries to also be emitted into install.sh scripts so that deployment is a single script run. This would let vars_kernel.tasks (and other generative subsystems) add LINKS that get co-authored into a shared install.sh, avoiding the need for separate manual symlink creation steps.

The install.sh pattern: build.sh generates files, install.sh deploys them (symlinks into system dirs). LINKS should feed into install.sh automatically.

title: Add dagger CLI .src.pb
description:

Dagger is a programmable CI/CD engine that runs pipelines as code in containers. The CLI binary is built from Go source.

The `.src.pb` should follow the compfuzor pattern for Go-based source builds:
- Set TYPE to `dagger`, REPO to `https://github.com/dagger/dagger`

- Import `tasks/compfuzor.includes`

title: Emit systemd sysext and confext layers
description:
Add support for generating systemd system extension (sysext) and configuration extension (confext) layers.

These are OS-level extension mechanisms in systemd that allow stacking additional filesystem layers on top of the base system:
- sysext: System extensions for adding binaries, libraries, and other system files
- confext: Configuration extensions for adding drop-in configuration

Both use raw GPT disk images with specific partition types and can be merged at runtime via systemd-sysext/systemd-confext.

title: Install usage.sh from sysctl-fs-inotify playbook; pin sysctls persistently
description:
`sysctl-fs-inotify.etc.pb` ships `files/fs-inotify/usage.sh` — a read-only per-user inotify watch/instance **top-consumer report** (the crucial diagnostic for the 2026-07-24 watchman/inotify incident) — as a `_bin` (`basedir: false` → `~/.local/bin`). The sysctl values are already at the playbook's targets (`max_user_watches=1048576`, `instances=8192`, `queued_events=65536`) but **`usage.sh` is not installed** (not on `PATH`, absent from `~/.local/bin`), so the top-consumers tool was unavailable when it was needed.

## Scope

- Apply `sysctl-fs-inotify.etc.pb` so `usage.sh` renders to `~/.local/bin` and is on `PATH`.
- Confirm sysctls are pinned persistently (a `/etc/sysctl.d` entry), not just set at runtime.
- Verify `usage.sh` (current user) and `usage.sh --sudo` (system-wide totals + top consumers) work.
- Cross-link `compfuzor-watchman-service`: `usage.sh` is how you see watchman/opencode burning watches.

## Acceptance

`usage.sh` on `PATH`; `usage.sh --help` works; sysctls persisted under `/etc/sysctl.d`; `usage.sh --sudo` shows system totals + top N consumers.

title: Audit when-clauses for redundant downstream defaults
description:
Many tasks guard with `when: X is defined` or `when: X is truthy` but then use `X|default(...)` downstream in the same task block. When the `when` already guarantees the variable exists/is truthy, the `default` filter is dead code that adds noise and cognitive load.

Example from `vars_repo.tasks`:
```yaml
when: \"REPOS is defined\"
with_items: \"{{(REPOS|default({})).keys()}}\"
```
The `when` ensures REPOS exists, so `|default({})` can never fire.

Scope: scan all `.tasks` files for patterns where a `when` condition proves a variable is defined/truthy but `|default(...)` is still used on that same variable within the task body. Also look for `|bool` casts on values already guaranteed boolean by the when-clause, and similar redundant defensive patterns.

This is a cleanup/refactoring pass — no behavior changes, just removing dead defaults and casts where the `when` clause already constrains the value.
